newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain must tackle tough health care reforms - govt.
newsitem.headline: Spain must tackle tough health care reforms - govt.

text.p: MADRID, Feb 21 - Spain must reform its health care system which absorbs five percent of gross domestic product and is devouring a growing part of public funds, Spain's Secretary of State for Social Security Juan Carlo Aparicio said on Friday.
But such reform is complicated by the fact that regional governments, now offering medical services to around 60 percent of the Spaniards, must be involved.
In 1996 Spain rehauled its pension system, reaching an agreement with trade unions, employers and the government.
"In the health care sector, it would be desirable to reach an agreement similar (to the pensions accord), but this is going to be more difficult," Aparicio told Reuters in a interview.
Aparicio said health care had to be reformed now to keep spending in line with expected Spanish economic growth and curb its growing social security deficit.
"We have to maintain expenditures in line with the expected growth, if not yearly, on a two-year basis," he added.

But the most difficult part would be to include regional governments in the talks. "...Given that 60 percent of the population is receiving health services from regional governments it is necessary that the deal includes them," Aparicio said.
Spain is expected to agree with regional governments this year a stability pact, intended to keep their spending under control.
Although it respected its public sector deficit target in 1996, Spain overshot its social security deficit target which was around 0.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), Aparicio added.
The 1996 deficit would be lower than in 1995, when it was 0.73 percent of GDP, he said, but still higher than the 0.3 percent target. Final figures are not yet available.

"We'll achieve an intermediate position (between the two figures), or a little lower, with a substantial fall in comparison with the previous year, and what is important is that we met the overall (public deficit) target of 4.4 percent," Aparicio said.

The total public deficit includes the central government deficit together with regional and local government and social security deficits. Spain's central government deficit was 3.3 percent of GDP in 1996, under the initial target of 3.5 percent.
The 1996 social security deficit could be "around 0.5 percent," Aparicio added.
Press reports have said the 1996 social security deficit was 372.6 billion pesetas ($2.6 billion) compared with a gross domestic product at 74.4 trillion pesetas.
Spain's social security deficit is expected to narrow more significantly this year. The government forecast in its 1997 budget that it would squeeze the deficit to 0.2 percent of GDP this year.
Aparicio did not give any forecast about the timing of health care reforms, saying only that "the agreement is desirable and possible, but very complex".
